newsitem.title: QATAR: Gulf Arabs to attack Israel at end of summit.
newsitem.headline: Gulf Arabs to attack Israel at end of summit.

text.p: Gulf Arab states are expected to accuse Israel on Monday of stalling the Middle East peace process and demand increased efforts by world powers to revive the talks, delegates said.
The final statement of the annual Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) summit is also expected to warn of a return to violence if the peace process started in 1991 collapses.
Like other Arab countries, GCC states accuse Israel of failing to honour peace accords signed with the Palestinians and blame it for the deadlock in talks with Syria and Lebanon.
GCC states, political and financial backers of the peace process, do not have diplomatic ties with Israel but members Oman and Qatar host Israeli trade offices.
The six-nation alliance also groups Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, United Arab Emirates and Bahrain.

Bahrain boycotted this year's summit over a territorial dispute with Qatar. The long-standing dispute between the two tiny states was exacerbated last week when Bahrain put two Qataris on trial for spying.

A wide range of military, political and economic issues have been discussed at the summit, which opened on Saturday. But delegates expect the leaders to refer once again to the planned unification of customs tariffs to the next summit, in Kuwait in late 1997.
The long-delayed step is crucial for the alliance reaching its target of a common market to facilitate free trade accords with major economic blocks.

"The summit has to agree on some of the issues under debate for many years or at least set a target date for implementation to absorb the frustration of their peoples with lack of action," said a senior Arab diplomat.
GCC states have taken some steps toward economic integration since the alliance was formed in 1981 but concrete measures have been blocked.
But on the political front they have maintained public unity despite often varying views on how to deal with their large neighbours Iraq and non-Arab Iran.

The final statement is expected to reiterate a call for Gulf War foe Iraq to implement all United Nations resolutions, including elimination of all its weapons of mass destruction and release of some 600 people Kuwait says Iraq is still holding.
But it was not clear how strong language would be on Iran, which GCC foreign ministers said earlier this year had military programmes that far exceed "conventional and legitimate" defence needs.
GCC Secretary-General Jameel al-Hujialan on Saturday defended the presence of U.S. and other Western forces in the oil-rich region to contain both Iraq and Iran.

"Arabs were the reason that Arabs sought the presence of these forces," he said of the controversial issue. "Unfortunately confidence is not available yet in Iraq...(and) some GCC states have political and military problems with Iran."
